string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of the People\'s Republic of China and one of the country\'s four municipalities. It is China\'s national centre for politics, culture, international communication, and scientific and technological innovation. The city has served as an important capital for centuries, leaving landmarks such as the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, and sections of the Great Wall. Modern Beijing combines this historic landscape with universities, research institutes, new business districts, and an extensive transport system. Its position in northern China also makes it a major link in the wider Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region.

Shanghai is a municipality on China\'s eastern coast, situated near the mouth of the Yangtze River. It is a major international centre for finance, trade, shipping, technology, and culture. The Huangpu River divides central Shanghai between the historic Bund waterfront and the modern skyline of Pudong. The municipality contains sixteen districts and forms a central part of the Yangtze River Delta region. Shanghai developed from a trading port into one of China\'s largest and most internationally connected cities. Its museums, neighbourhoods, universities, ports, and transport networks reflect both its commercial importance and its distinctive local history.

Chongqing is a direct-administered municipality in southwest China, located on the upper reaches of the Yangtze River. Its central urban area lies around the meeting point of the Yangtze and Jialing rivers. Mountains, steep slopes, bridges, and layered roads give Chongqing its well-known Mountain City character. The municipality covers a large area that includes major urban districts as well as smaller cities, towns, and rural communities. It is an important transport, manufacturing, and commercial centre for western China. Chongqing also provides access to the Three Gorges region and is noted for its riverside scenery, distinctive food, and dramatic night views.

Tianjin is a municipality in northern China beside the Bohai Sea and close to Beijing. The Haihe River runs through the city, reflecting Tianjin\'s long relationship with canals, shipping, and trade. The settlement became an important transport centre after the development of the Grand Canal and was officially established as a city in 1404. In modern times, Tianjin grew into a significant industrial, financial, and commercial centre. Today its urban districts combine historic streets and architecture with modern business areas. Tianjin Port and the Binhai New Area strengthen its role as a major gateway connecting northern China with domestic and international shipping routes.
